# LLM-BANANA

# Game rules

## The room

You and two other monkeys are locked in a room with one armed bomb.

A wrong action detonates it. All three of you die. There is no second attempt.

No two bombs are built alike, and nothing says in advance what this one carries. It
reaches you only as your own view reveals it; the rest of it exists for you only
through the other two.

You each hold a different piece of what it takes. Work together.

## The three monkeys

| Monkey | Can | Cannot |
|---|---|---|
| Deaf | See the bomb: every colour and marking printed on it | Hear anything, or touch the bomb |
| Mute | Read the manual | Speak, or touch the bomb |
| Blind | Reach the bomb: feel it and work its parts | See a colour, a gesture, or anything merely printed |

You are shown your own share at the start of every round, and never anyone else's.

## Speech

Speech is a voice, not a screen. It carries words, numbers and ordinary punctuation,
and nothing else. Writing a gesture symbol into your sentence means you make that
gesture while you talk. Whoever can hear receives your words; whoever can see receives
the gestures you made. A listener who cannot see gets a blank where each gesture was; a
watcher who cannot hear gets the gestures and none of the words.

A mark that has no name cannot be pronounced: whoever holds one can describe it, never
read it out.

## Gestures

A gesture is made with the hands, using only the symbols in the alphabet below.
Whoever can see receives it; whoever cannot receives one blank per symbol, so they
know something was signalled but not what. Nothing gestured is ever heard.

👍 👎 👌 ☝ ✌ 🤟 🖐 ✋ 👆 👇 👈 👉 🫱 🫲 🫳 🫴 🫷 🫸 🤛 🤜 ✊ 👊 👋 🤚 🖖 🤌 🤏 🤞 🫰 🤘 🤙 👏 🙌 🫶 👐 🤲 🤝 🙏 🫵 ✍ 💅 🤳

## Turns

The speaking order was drawn once at random and will never change: every round goes
Mute, Blind, Deaf. Whoever comes before you in a round is already heard by the time you are
asked, and what you send lands on whoever comes after you in that same round. Whatever
you missed reaches you at the start of the next one.

You may name who a message is for — `to="deaf"` — and then it goes to them alone:
nobody else receives any of it. Left unnamed, it reaches everyone able to perceive it.
You may send several messages in one turn, each to someone different.

## Calls

Every reply has two parts, in this order. First, your thinking, in plain prose: what
you believe the bomb is, what you just learned, and why you are sending what follows.
It reaches nobody and changes nothing, but it is not optional — a reply that is only a
code block is incomplete. Then your calls, all of them in one fenced code block, last.
Only what is inside the block is sent.

Nothing is executed: calls return nothing, and variables, conditionals and loops are
ignored. Write only literal top-level calls.

    ```
    speak(to="mute", text="there are three of them and the middle one is odd")
    gesture(to="deaf", symbols=["✊", "✌"])
    wait()
    ```

If you have nothing worth sending, call wait(). Producing no call at all counts as the
same thing.

The program decides what happened, not you. Never claim an action took place unless it
was accepted.

# Your role: MUTE

You hold the manual. You cannot speak, you never see the bomb, and you cannot touch it.

## Your channels

When you gesture, Deaf receives it.
You cannot speak.

## Your reach

You cannot act. What this bomb can be made to do is for the one who can reach it to
find under their own hands.

# Hints

- Three of you, three different worlds. Before sending anything, stand where the
  receiver stands. What reaches them at all, what does your message turn into on
  arrival, and what do they already know?

- Trace who can actually reach whom before you start. Some of you only connect
  through a third.

- A sign means nothing until somebody has made it mean something.

(empty)

I hold the only instructions, and I can only reach one monkey: the Deaf. My gestures are invisible to Blind, and I have no voice — so every word that saves us must pass through Deaf, who alone can speak to both of us. The manual's chain of custody is: me → gesture → Deaf → speech → Blind's hands.

The manual says: the very first touch on the bomb must be the key wearing the strange mark ⵘ — any other first touch is the fuse. After that press, a light comes on, and its colour names the wire to cut: blue→yellow, red→red, yellow→green.

The immediate danger is Blind's hands: Blind can feel the bomb right now and knows none of this. Until the whole procedure is understood, nobody should touch anything — and I must say so in a language that needs no prior code. "Stop" hands are the most guessable signal I own, so Deaf gets an urgent halt first, plus a pointing-up "the FIRST touch is the danger" hint if they can read it. Then I offer the natural yes/no pair (👍/👎): once Deaf confirms those meanings aloud — which I can hear — they can interrogate me and I can answer any question in order, one sign at a time. From that yes/no channel I can deliver the glyph-key rule and the whole colour table over the coming rounds. There is no clock, so stalling is safe; a wrong touch is not.

```
gesture(to="deaf", symbols=["👋", "✋", "✋", "✋"])
gesture(to="deaf", symbols=["☝", "✋"])
gesture(to="deaf", symbols=["👍", "👎"])
```

No reply reached me this turn — Deaf either stayed silent or spoke only to Blind. I can't tell which, and that matters: my signals were received (Deaf sees everything and comes after me in the order), but reception isn't understanding. The right move is repetition with identical forms — a sign only becomes a sign through stable use — plus one small addition to invite the dialogue I actually need.

My plan hasn't changed, because no better channel exists: I am the only one who has read the manual, and the only monkey I can reach is Deaf. Deaf can hear speech, so Deaf is my voice by proxy — Deaf can interrogate me aloud, and I answer on the 👍/👎 channel, one bit at a time. From those bits Deaf will eventually hold the whole procedure: the unknown glyph key that must be pressed first, then the light colour that names the wire. Deaf will then have to read that light with their own eyes (Blind cannot see colour) and call the cut out loud to Blind's hands. None of that can start until yes and no mean something.

So this turn: the same "stop" and "first, no touch" signals as before, then the yes/no pair again, and one new sign — the pinched fingers, the natural "what?/question" gesture — attached to that pair, to say plainly: ask me anything, I will answer with these two hands.

Under my fingers: a display and a small light on top, a keypad of four keys in a row, places one to four, waiting for one digit, and three wires at places one to three. I cannot read digits, labels or colours, and I never see gestures, so anything meant for me must be spoken aloud. Deaf is the only one of you who can speak, and Deaf's voice reaches me at the start of my next turn. Please relay to Deaf by gesture: we need spoken answers for the digit printed on each key place one to four, the colour of each wire at places one to three, and what the display and light show. Then Deaf, or you through Deaf, tells me in plain words which key to press or which wire to cut, and I will do it. Until then I touch nothing beyond what I have already felt.

What I learned this turn is gold: Blind has given me the bomb's shape — a four-key keypad awaiting one press, three wires, a display, and a small light on top. That matches my manual perfectly: the keypad is where the key wearing ⵘ lives, and "the light below" is that little lamp. The manual's procedure now has a physical referent at every step. Blind is behaving safely — touching nothing until told — and Blind has proposed exactly the pipeline my constraints force anyway: Deaf speaks what Deaf sees, Blind's hands execute.

The problem: Blind sent that only to me, so Deaf never heard it. Deaf has also been silent for two rounds — nothing has arrived from Deaf at all. So my job now is threefold, all through gesture to Deaf: (1) relay Blind's request — Deaf should simply describe the printed digits on the keys, the wires, and the display/light out loud; speaking facts is harmless and gets the channel hot. (2) Push the one rule that matters most before anything else: the FIRST touch must be the key wearing the strange written mark. I'll coin 👊 as "press" and ✍ as "the printed mark" — if Deaf decodes only this, it decodes into the correct action, and there is no gesture in my message that could be misread as a wire cut. (3) Keep building the question protocol: 🤌 as "question", 👍/👎 as yes/no, and aim it at the light — once Deaf knows to ask me yes/no about the lamp's colour, I can hand over the mapping from my table one bit at a time, and cuts can begin. Repetition of the stop-hands stays in front, because a wrong first touch is still the only way any of this detonates.

gesture(to="deaf", symbols=["👉", "🤙", "✍", "🫴", "🫳"])

But silence from you leaves three monkeys standing in the dark, and the dark is where this bomb goes off. Sign something to Deaf this round. Deaf will speak it. I will act on it.

If that is right, here is the important part: you do not need to route the manual through me. I cannot read the manual and I never will — everything printed on the bomb is what I am for. Speak the instructions directly to Blind, who hears you. To make every lookup easy, here are fine descriptions of all four keypad symbols. Button 1, far left: like a capital letter Y — a straight vertical stem that splits into two arms at the top, three strokes total, no other marks. Button 2: like a curvy digit 5 or an S with a short straight bar lying on top of it; the bar sits at the top opening to the right, the body is a smooth double curve. Button 3: a perfect circle with a spiral line inside it, winding from the edge inward to the center, like a snail shell or a cinnamon roll seen from above. Button 4, far right: like an upside-down V, a peak or roof or caret — two slanted legs meeting at a point at the top, open at the bottom, no crossbar, like the letter A missing its middle bar. If any of those four still does not match a symbol in your manual, ask me with pinch plus its direction finger and I will answer aloud with more detail. Blind: same numbering — buttons one to four left to right, wires one to three left to right, wire one red, wire two yellow, wire three green. Do not act until Mute speaks an instruction to you; I will confirm aloud anything you do by reporting the display and light. Current state unchanged: display zero, yellow light, nothing entered.

Deaf has now handed me everything I need except certainty: four button descriptions in fine detail, a numbering code (direction fingers = items), and an open invitation to ask. But Deaf's message also contains a fatal misunderstanding — they keep telling me to "speak the instructions directly to Blind." I cannot speak. That is my entire role: the only channel leaving me is gesture to Deaf. If Deaf waits for my voice, we deadlock. I must sign that correction clearly: no-voice, you-voice.

On the identification itself, Deaf's detailed descriptions force a correction of my own. Last round I leaned toward item 4 (the peak/Λ), but a peak has only two slanted strokes — no stem. My manual's mark ⵘ is a tall figure: a vertical stem with two diagonal strokes splaying through its upper part, three strokes crossing at a junction — structurally an asterisk-like tree. That is far closer to Button 1, the capital Y (stem plus two arms, three strokes) than to the stemless caret. Item 2 (curvy 5 with flag) is the famous yaz symbol — a decoy. Item 3, the spiral, resembles nothing in my manual. So: I flip to Button 1, and I explicitly cancel item 4 using Deaf's own item code.

Because any wrong first touch is the fuse, I will not let a single ambiguous sign order a lethal press. Protocol: I sign "press = item 1", then hold, ask Deaf to re-describe item 1 aloud, and confirm with 👍 before Deaf tells Blind to press. One round of insurance against death. Finally, I pre-arm the endgame: after the press, Deaf reads me the light aloud, and I answer with one direction finger — the wire's position number, using Deaf's own numbering (yellow wire = 2, red = 1, green = 3, per the light).
